facts.fact_text: The applicants are a group of individuals and the Foundation for Equality.
The applicants wished to hold an assembly (a march) in Warsaw within the framework of Equality Days organised by the Foundation for Equality, planned for 10-12 June 2005.

The purpose of the planned march in Warsaw was to alert public opinion to the issue of discrimination against minorities – sexual, national, ethnic and religious – and also against women and disabled persons.
On 3 June 2005 the applicants informed the Mayor of Warsaw about stationary assemblies they intended to hold on 11 June 2005 in seven different squares in Warsaw.

Four of the seven planned stationary assemblies on 11 June 2005 were intended to protest about discrimination against various minorities and to support actions of groups and organisations combating discrimination.
Three of the seven planned stationary assemblies on 11 June 2005 were intended to protest about discrimination against women.
On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.
The march on 11 June 2005 was attended by approximately 3,000 people.
The march on 11 June 2005 was protected by the police.
On 3 June 2005 the Traffic Officer, acting on behalf of the Mayor of Warsaw, refused permission for the march.

On 9 June 2005 the Mayor of Warsaw issued decisions banning the stationary assemblies to be organised by Mr Bączkowski, Mr Biedroń, Mr Kliszczyński, Ms Kostrzewa, Mr Szypuła, and Mr N. (who is not an applicant).
Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, the lodging of an appeal against a refusal of permission to hold a demonstration does not have a suspensive effect on the refusal.
On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.

On 11 May 2005 Mr Bączkowski obtained an instruction of the Warsaw Mayor's Office on requirements which organisers of public assemblies have to comply with under the Road Traffic Act, applicable should the assembly be regarded as an 'event' (impreza) within the meaning of Article 65 of the Road Traffic Act.

The Traffic Officer's refusal of permission for the march on 3 June 2005 was based on the organisers' failure to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') within the meaning of Article 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act.
On 22 August 2005 the Local Government Appeals Board quashed the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission for the march, finding that it was unlawful.

The Local Government Appeals Board observed that under the applicable provisions of administrative procedure the authorities were obliged to ensure that parties to administrative proceedings had an opportunity of effectively participating in them.

The Local Government Appeals Board found that the obligation to ensure effective participation in administrative proceedings had not been respected in the applicant Foundation for Equality's case, in that the case file contained no evidence that the applicant Foundation for Equality had been informed of its procedural right to have access to the case file.

The Local Government Appeals Board found that the first-instance authority's decision of 3 June 2005 referred to the absence of a traffic organisation plan in the case file, but that the case file contained no mention that the organisers had been obliged to submit such a plan.

The Local Government Appeals Board found that the document on the procedure for obtaining permission to organise an event which was served on the organisers contained no information on the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan.
On 17 June 2005 the Mazowsze Governor quashed the Mayor of Warsaw's refusals of 9 June 2005 of authorisation to hold the stationary assemblies.

The Mazowsze Governor observed that the Mayor of Warsaw's decisions of 9 June 2005 breached the law in that the parties had been served only with copies of the decisions, not with originals as required by the law on administrative procedure.

The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw had informed the media of his decisions of 9 June 2005 before they had been served on the applicants, which was manifestly in breach of the principles of administrative procedure.
The Mazowsze Governor observed that the applicable law did not provide for any permit for the holding of an assembly.

The Mazowsze Governor noted that the requirement to submit a permit to occupy a part of the road, based on the provisions of the Road Traffic Act, lacked any legal basis in the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act.

Under section 65 of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, the organisers of sporting events, contests, assemblies and other events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to obtain permission for the organisation of such assemblies.

Under section 65 read together with section 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, organisers of events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to comply with various administrative obligations specified in a list contained in section 65(a), numbering nineteen items, including the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan to the authorities.
The Constitutional Court concluded in its judgment of 18 January 2006 that section 65 of the Road Traffic Act was incompatible with the Constitution in so far as it applied to assemblies.

The Traffic Officer's refusal of permission for the march on 3 June 2005 was based on the organisers' failure to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') within the meaning of Article 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act.

In his decision of 9 June 2005 banning the stationary assemblies, the Mayor of Warsaw relied on the argument that assemblies held under the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act (Ustawa o zgromadzeniach) had to be organised away from roads used for road traffic.
In his decision of 9 June 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that if assemblies were to use roads, more stringent requirements applied.
The organisers of the stationary assemblies wished to use cars carrying loudspeakers.
The organisers had failed to indicate where and how the cars carrying loudspeakers would park during the assemblies so as not to disturb traffic.
The organisers had failed to indicate how the movement of persons and cars between the assembly sites would be organised.
The Mayor of Warsaw refused permission for the applicants' stationary assemblies in part to avoid possible violent clashes between participants in the various demonstrations planned for 11 June 2005.

The Mayor of Warsaw refused permission for the applicants' stationary assemblies in part to avoid possible violent clashes between participants in the various demonstrations planned for 11 June 2005.

On 9 June 2005 the municipal authorities, acting on the Mayor of Warsaw's behalf, allowed the three planned stationary assemblies concerning discrimination against women to be held as requested by the applicants.
On 9 June 2005 the municipal authorities, acting on the Mayor of Warsaw's behalf, permitted six other demonstrations to be held on 11 June 2005.

The six other demonstrations permitted on 9 June 2005 to be held on 11 June 2005 had the following themes: 'For more stringent measures against persons convicted of paedophilia', 'Against any legislative work on the law on partnerships', 'Against propaganda for partnerships', 'Education in Christian values, a guarantee of a moral society', 'Christians respecting God's and nature's laws are citizens of the first rank', and 'Against adoption of children by homosexual couples'.
On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.
The march on 11 June 2005 followed the itinerary as planned in the original request of 12 May 2005.
The march on 11 June 2005 was attended by approximately 3,000 people.
The march on 11 June 2005 was protected by the police.
On 22 August 2005 the Local Government Appeals Board quashed the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission for the march, finding that it was unlawful.
On 17 June 2005 the Mazowsze Governor quashed the Mayor of Warsaw's refusals of 9 June 2005 of authorisation to hold the stationary assemblies.

The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw had assumed that the demonstration would occupy a part of the road, but had failed to take any steps to clarify whether this had really been the organisers' intention, which he was obliged to do by law.
The Mazowsze Governor observed that a decision banning an assembly had to be regarded as a method of last resort because it radically restricted freedom of expression.

The Mazowsze Governor observed that the principle of proportionality required that any restriction of constitutionally protected freedoms be permitted only in so far as it was dictated by the concrete circumstances of a particular case.

The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw's reliance on the threat of violence between the demonstrations organised by the applicants and the counter-demonstrations planned by other persons and organisations for 11 June 2005 could not be countenanced.

The Mazowsze Governor stated that the Mayor of Warsaw's reliance on the threat of violence was tantamount to the administration endorsing the intentions of organisations which clearly and deliberately intended to breach public order.
The Mazowsze Governor stated that protecting the freedom of expression guaranteed by the 1990 Assemblies Act should be an essential task of the public powers.
In the interview published in 'Gazeta Wyborcza' on 20 May 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that he had not read the organisers' application.
In the interview published in 'Gazeta Wyborcza' on 20 May 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that he would ban the demonstration regardless of what the organisers had written in their application.

In the interview published in 'Gazeta Wyborcza' on 20 May 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that he was not for discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation, for example by ruining people's professional careers, but that there would be no public propaganda about homosexuality.

In the interview published in 'Gazeta Wyborcza' on 20 May 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that he did not forbid the organisers to demonstrate if they wanted to demonstrate as citizens, not as homosexuals.
In the interview published in 'Gazeta Wyborcza' on 20 May 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that he would not let himself be persuaded to give permission for such a demonstration.
In the interview published in 'Gazeta Wyborcza' on 20 May 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that in his view propaganda about homosexuality was not the same as exercising one's freedom of assembly.
